opening_attribution:
A political remembrance of Ba’athist Iraq.
Narration preserves the supplied advocacy text; factual qualifications appear on screen.
required_context_caption:
Development coexisted with dictatorship.
The 1988 Anfal campaign targeted Kurdish civilians.
requirements: Preserve spoken text only with clear attribution as political remembrance, not an unqualified factual account.
Show each material correction legibly at its corresponding spoken claim; do not rely on a generic disclaimer.
Do not show an unrelated year or place as if it records the narrated event.
Include the documented repression/Anfal context before the Arabic-only final card.
Keep the final eight-second Arabic-only hold free of English corrections.
If corrections cannot fit legibly, publication remains blocked until narration is revised or the format is changed.

claims.match_text: June 1st 1972. Iraq nationalized its oil.
claims.reason: 1 June nationalized IPC assets in northern Iraq; affiliated Mosul and Basrah operations were excluded from that decree.
claims.caption:
1 JUNE 1972 · IPC nationalized
Other oil holdings followed later.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: June 1st, 1972. Iraq nationalized the Iraq Petroleum Company.

claims.match_text: The wealth extracted for fifty years by British Petroleum — came home.
claims.reason: BP was one consortium shareholder (23.75%). The 1925 concession predates 1972 by 47 years; it is not evidence of fifty years of BP extraction.
claims.caption:
IPC was a multinational consortium.
BP held 23.75%; the concession dated to 1925.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: The assets of a foreign-owned consortium, including British Petroleum, passed to the Iraqi state.

claims.match_text: Per capita income tripled.
claims.reason: Nominal GDP/person nearly tripled between 1972 and 1975; real GDP/person rose about 23% in that interval. GDP is not personal income; nationalization alone does not establish causality.
claims.caption:
GDP/person, 1972–75: nearly 3× in current US$.
Inflation-adjusted growth: about 23%.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: Between 1972 and 1975, nominal GDP per person nearly tripled.

claims.match_text: Every child received free education through university.
claims.reason: State education was tuition-free through higher education. That does not mean every child attended university; postprimary study was optional.
claims.caption:
Education was tuition-free through university.
Attendance and access were not universal.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: State education was free through university, though access remained unequal.

claims.match_text: Every citizen received free healthcare.
claims.reason: A free public healthcare system existed, but entitlement is not proof every citizen actually received every needed service.
claims.caption:
Public healthcare was provided free of charge.
This did not guarantee care reached everyone.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: Public healthcare was free, supported by expanding hospitals and clinics.

claims.match_text: UNESCO awarded Iraq its literacy prize.
claims.reason: 1979 Krupskaya award recognizes the national literacy campaign, not proof illiteracy disappeared. State report explicitly records award.
claims.caption:
1979 · UNESCO Krupskaya literacy prize
Awarded for Iraq’s national literacy campaign.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: In 1979, UNESCO’s Krupskaya prize recognized Iraq’s literacy campaign.

claims.match_text: The Arab world watched and understood — this is what sovereignty looks like.
claims.reason: Regional reactions were not uniform. OPEC approved the nationalization but governments differed over cooperation.
claims.caption:
The narration voices a pan-Arab interpretation.
Regional governments responded differently.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: Supporters across the Arab world saw a declaration of sovereignty.

claims.match_text: Ba’athism answered the oldest question — what does the Arab nation owe itself? Everything.
claims.reason: Normative question and answer; attribute to a political voice, never to a historical finding.
claims.caption:
BA’ATHIST IDEOLOGY
Arab unity · liberation · socialism
claims.suggested_revised_narration: Ba’athism promised Arab unity, liberation and socialism.

claims.match_text: Its language taught without shame.
claims.reason: Cultural pride is a political sentiment; Arabic teaching does not establish freedom for all linguistic communities.
claims.caption:
Cultural pride was part of the party’s message.
Iraq also contained non-Arab peoples and languages.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: It promised dignity for Arabic language and culture.

claims.match_text: Its women standing in every courtroom, every hospital, every military rank.
claims.reason: Women gained education and professional opportunities. No evidence establishes all courtrooms, hospitals, or every military rank. Persistent discrimination and party control preclude the universal wording.
claims.caption:
Women gained educational and professional roles.
“Every military rank” is not substantiated.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: Women entered more classrooms, hospitals and professional workplaces.

claims.match_text: A Christian as Foreign Minister.
claims.reason: Tariq Aziz was a Chaldean Christian and Foreign Minister 1983–91, not Foreign Minister in 1972.
claims.caption:
TARIQ AZIZ · Chaldean Christian
Foreign Minister, 1983–1991
claims.suggested_revised_narration: Tariq Aziz, a Christian, became Foreign Minister in 1983.

claims.match_text: A farmer owning his land.
claims.reason: Agrarian reform existed, including 1970 law; land redistribution began before Baath rule in 1958. Not all farmers owned land.
claims.caption:
Land reform began in 1958.
The Ba’ath government extended it in 1970.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: Agrarian reform redistributed land, continuing changes begun in 1958.

claims.match_text: One secular state. One Arab identity. No foreign permission required.
claims.reason: Describes secular pan-Arab aspirations. Does not describe all identities or imply freedom from state coercion, religious family law, external dependence, or political opposition.
claims.caption:
A secular, pan-Arab state was the ideal.
Iraq’s people held diverse identities.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: It proclaimed a secular state and a common Arab identity.

claims.match_text: They called Ba’athism dangerous. They were right.
claims.reason: No specified speaker, date or quotation. A political judgment rather than a documented universal reaction.
claims.caption: “Dangerous” is the narrator’s political judgment.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: To its supporters, these changes challenged the established order.

claims.match_text: A sovereign Arab state that nationalized its oil threatened every company grown rich on Arab resources.
claims.reason: Conflicts over IPC compensation and marketing are documented; every company feeling threatened cannot be verified.
claims.caption:
IPC owners contested compensation and oil sales.
“Every company” is an interpretation.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: Nationalization challenged foreign owners and their control of oil sales.

claims.match_text: An educated Arab population threatened every power that depended on Arab dependency.
claims.reason: No defined powers, mechanism, date or evidence establishes the universal motive.
claims.caption:
A political interpretation of education and power,
not a documented motive shared by all states.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: Its supporters saw education as a route away from dependency.

claims.match_text: They called it instability. Stability for whom?
claims.reason: Unspecified critics and an interpretive question; cannot be presented as a sourced quotation.
claims.caption:
The question is political rhetoric.
The government also violently repressed opposition.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: Yet development coexisted with dictatorship and violent repression.

claims.match_text: The oil was Arab. The schools were full.
claims.reason: State oil ownership and educational expansion support a symbolic closing, not ethnic ownership or universal school attendance.
claims.caption:
State oil ownership and expanding schools
coexisted with unequal access and state control.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: Oil revenues supported new schools and public services.

claims.match_text: The women were free.
claims.reason: Professional gains did not equal unrestricted political, civil, or family freedom. Discrimination and repression persisted.
claims.caption:
Women’s opportunities expanded.
Equal rights and political freedom remained limited.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: Women gained opportunities, while discrimination and repression endured.

claims.match_text: The borders were challenged. Remember that Iraq.
claims.reason: Can refer to pan-Arab aims; do not euphemize expansionist wars or imply this is the whole history of Iraq.
claims.caption:
Pan-Arab unity was an aspiration.
Iraq also waged devastating wars.
claims.suggested_revised_narration: Remember the achievements, and the human cost of that Iraq.

sources.title: Some Implications of Iraq’s Oil Nationalization, June 1972
sources.publisher: US Department of State, Office of the Historian; contemporary CIA memorandum ER IM 72–92
sources.retrieval: Full page read; primary contemporary intelligence source. Its predictions and political judgments are attributed assessments, not neutral facts.

sources.title: Iraq report on ICESCR articles 13–15, E/1982/3/Add.26
sources.publisher: Republic of Iraq, submitted to the United Nations
sources.retrieval: Original English PDF downloaded and pdftotext-extracted. A government self-report is primary evidence for stated law/policy and the reported award, not independent evidence of universal outcomes.

sources.title: World Development Indicators: Iraq GDP per capita, current US$
sources.retrieval: JSON API retrieved directly. Values: 394.41834302923 and 1165.88163945653; ratio 2.95595185. GDP per capita is not household income.

sources.title: World Development Indicators: Iraq GDP per capita, constant US$
sources.retrieval: JSON API retrieved directly. Values: 1325.75580274961 and 1633.76336398088; ratio 1.23232597; +23.23%. Revision-vintage may change exact values.

sources.title: Background on Women’s Status in Iraq Prior to the Fall of the Saddam Hussein Government
sources.locator: Women’s Status in Iraq Prior to the 1991 Gulf War; footnotes 9, 12, 15, 21
sources.retrieval: Full page read. Primary NGO investigation/synthesis distinguishes legal and workplace gains from discrimination and state control.

sources.title: Support to Emergency Obstetric Care in Iraq: External Evaluation Report
sources.publisher: Report submitted to UNFPA, Stars Orbit Consultants, April–May 2010 evaluation
sources.retrieval: Full 60-page PDF accessed through UNDP host. Historical paragraph records free centrally administered care and later deterioration.

sources.title: Tariq Aziz — Iraq, 9 November 1993 profile
sources.retrieval: Indexed text retrieved in web search: Foreign Affairs 1983–91; Chaldean Christian. Direct live document URL redirects to maintenance/Reading Room, so corroborated against S8 and S9.

sources.title: Secretary-General’s report on visit to Iran and Iraq, S/17097
sources.retrieval: Indexed original UN PDF text identifies Tariq Aziz as Foreign Minister in 1985.

sources.title: Former Saddam-Era Minister Tariq Aziz Dies
sources.publisher: Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, 5 June 2015; AFP, Reuters, BBC reporting
sources.retrieval: Indexed article text corroborates Christian identity and 1983–91 Foreign Minister term.

sources.title: Iraq’s Crime of Genocide: The Anfal Campaign against the Kurds
sources.publisher: Human Rights Watch and Yale University Press, 1994
sources.retrieval: Full page read. Investigation used captured Iraqi government records and survivor testimony; documents genocide and destruction of Kurdish communities in 1988.

sources.title: FAO Conference: Thirteenth Meeting, statement by I.I. Azzawi (Iraq)
sources.publisher: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, 1983 conference proceedings
sources.locator: Iraqi delegation statement, agrarian reform passage
sources.retrieval: Full page read. Primary state statement describes 1970 and 1975 land laws; it is evidence of official policy/claims, not proof that every farmer owned land.

sources.title: The Metaphysical Universe of Michel ʿAflaq and His Party: A Reappraisal of the Baʿth
sources.publisher: Modern Intellectual History, Cambridge University Press
sources.retrieval: Indexed scholarly text; interpretive secondary source, cites primary writings. Supports attribution to ideology, not factual endorsement.

sources.title: Iraq Petroleum Company: House of Commons debate, 5 June 1972
sources.retrieval: Indexed contemporary parliamentary statement corroborates 1 June IPC nationalization.

sources.title: Recent changes in agrarian reform and rural development strategies in the Near East
sources.publisher: M. Riad El-Ghonemy, FAO Land Reform
sources.retrieval: Full page read. Records Iraq reform dates 1958 and 1971; documents incomplete redistribution and subsequent military spending.

sources.title: Report of the Commission Entrusted by the Council with the Study of the Frontier between Syria and Iraq
sources.publisher: Library of Congress, League of Nations historical item
sources.retrieval: Indexed Library of Congress catalogue summary: 1920 Anglo-French convention and subsequent boundary commission.

sources.title: Just a Line in the Sand? The Making of an Arabian Border, 1925
sources.publisher: Qatar Digital Library / British Library, William Monk, 24 March 2021
sources.retrieval: Indexed institutional archival interpretation; cautions that modern frontiers were not simply the Sykes-Picot map and involved multiple negotiations.

research_limitations: Firecrawl search could not run: connected account was out of credits. Used available web search and direct institutional retrieval.

UNESCO original 1979 award booklet URL was discovered but live access returned HTTP 403. Award was corroborated with original UN-hosted Iraqi state report E/1982/3/Add.26 p.10 and contemporary reporting. Exact Supreme Council recipient wording appears in bibliographic sources; do not inflate the award into certification that all Iraqis were literate.
CIA live biography redirects to maintenance/Reading Room; indexed content was cross-checked against original UN Foreign Minister identification and independent biography.
No evidence found for women holding every military rank.

opening_card_claims.match_text: They drew your borders without asking.
opening_card_claims.reason: Colonial powers shaped borders, but modern Iraq’s boundaries were settled through multiple commissions, negotiations and conflicts; the line is not a literal summary of a single agreement.
opening_card_claims.caption:
Britain and France shaped borders under mandate.
Boundaries emerged through several later agreements.

opening_card_claims.match_text: They took your oil without sharing.
opening_card_claims.reason: Iraq received oil royalties and revenue before nationalization; nationalization changed ownership and control.
opening_card_claims.caption:
Iraq already received oil revenues.
Nationalization changed ownership and control.

opening_card_claims.reason: Oil concessions were curtailed by Law 80 in 1961, before the 1968 Baath takeover. Nationalization in 1972 continued an older struggle.
opening_card_claims.caption:
Law 80 restricted concessions in 1961,
before the Ba’ath Party took lasting power in 1968.
